reason: The current goal is to make a muscle fibre pull, so I’ll start by adding its structures to the cell.
expectation: I expect an elongated muscle fibre retaining the cell’s membrane and mitochondria, but it may still need filament machinery to pull.

alternatives.reason: Attaching the triceps could help build the arm, but the fibre goal comes first.

effect: The cell is now an elongated muscle fibre with spaces for contractile units, so adding filaments is the next step toward pulling.
reaction: The retained cell structures make the connection between chapters clear.
reason: Sliding filaments appear to be the fibre’s pulling machinery.
expectation: I expect the filaments to fit into the fibre, though a calcium signal may still be needed for contraction.

alternatives.reason: The triceps could be attached to the skeleton, but I want to complete the fibre goal first.

effect: The fibre now has ATP-ready filaments, but the actin grip sites remain covered; the calcium signal looks like the next step toward pulling.
reaction: The inset makes the distinction between a reset myosin head and an attached one clear.
reason: Add the calcium signal to see how it enables the filaments to pull.
expectation: I expect calcium to expose the grip sites so myosin can attach and the fibre can contract; it may still need a separate reset step.

alternatives.reason: Attaching the triceps remains useful for the arm, but the fibre goal is still unfinished.

effect: Calcium exposed the grip sites, allowing the myosin cycle to slide the filaments; the fibre still needs to become ready again.
reaction: The distinction between sliding filaments and shortening filaments is a useful clarification.
reason: Use the calcium-pumping membranes to help reset the fibre after contraction.
expectation: I expect the pumps to move calcium back into storage using ATP, allowing the fibre to relax and become ready again.

alternatives.reason: The triceps can help build the arm, but the current fibre goal still needs its reset.

effect: The fibre has stopped pulling and is ready to respond again; the new goal shifts attention to opposing muscle pulls on the bones.
reaction: It is useful to see that relaxation requires ATP-powered calcium pumping and an outside pull to lengthen the fibre.
reason: Gathering fibres seems like a practical next step toward building a muscle that can pull on the arm.
expectation: I expect a group of muscle fibres, which may still need connective tissue and attachment to the skeleton.

alternatives.reason: Attaching the triceps also serves the new goal, but I want to build up the fibre first.

effect: The fibre is now part of a parallel bundle, linking the earlier filament model to a larger muscle structure.
reaction: The paired poses help connect individual fibres to the bundle’s movement.
reason: Add the connective tissue sheaths to continue building a muscle that can transmit a pull.
expectation: I expect the bundle to be wrapped in connective tissue, possibly providing a route toward a tendon attachment.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also belongs in the arm, but I want to finish building the bundle first.

effect: The fibre bundle is now a biceps with tendons that can carry its pull to bone; it still needs attachment to the skeleton.
reaction: The sheaths gathering into tendons make the link from fibres to bone clear.
reason: Attach the newly built biceps to the arm skeleton to advance the opposing-pulls goal.
expectation: I expect the biceps tendons to attach to the bones so shortening can bend the elbow; the triceps may still need to be added.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs attaching, but I want to connect the biceps I just built first.

effect: The biceps is attached and shown bending the elbow; the empty extensor slot points to adding the triceps.
reaction: The two poses make the biceps’ pull on the forearm clear.
reason: Fit the triceps into the extensor slot; it is the only offered combination and should provide the opposing pull.
expectation: I expect the triceps to attach across the elbow and help straighten the arm, though the assembly may still need blood vessels.

effect: The triceps now supplies the opposing pull, straightening the elbow as it shortens. The assembly still has an offered blood-vessel combination.
reaction: The paired poses make the opposing actions of the two muscles clear.
reason: Add the limb blood vessels; it is the only offered combination and may supply the working muscles.
expectation: I expect vessels to branch through the arm and connect muscle activity to its fuel and oxygen supply, though I am unsure whether this completes the goal.

effect: The vessels complete the muscular arm and its goal, while their unconnected ends point toward a larger circulation.
reaction: The vessel inset usefully connects the arm’s muscles back to cellular ATP production, though the supply route remains incomplete.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the calcium signal was most worthwhile: the planned cycle distinguishes myosin attachment, pulling, release and reset, while showing that filaments slide rather than shorten.

leastWorthwhile.text: Gathering the other fibres into a bundle was less engaging than the surrounding steps; it mainly scaled up the structure without explaining much new.

surprise.text: Relaxation also requires ATP-powered calcium pumping, and the fibre lengthens under an outside pull rather than pushing itself back.

arbitrary.text: The bundle becoming a complete biceps with tendons after adding sheaths felt like a large jump in scale, although the result explains how connective tissue carries the pull into tendons.

continue.text: I would continue to see how the unfinished vessel ends connect to circulation. The chapter’s links from ATP to contraction and opposing muscle pulls made that progression interesting, although these illustration plans do not establish student comprehension.
